canonical_identity.abstract: The remarkable evolution of generative models has enabled the generation of high-quality, visually attractive images, often perceptually indistinguishable from real photographs to human eyes. This has spurred significant attention on AI-generated image (AIGI) detection. Intuitively, higher image quality should increase detection difficulty. However, our systematic study on cutting-edge text-to-image generators reveals a counterintuitive finding: AIGIs with higher quality scores, as assessed by human preference models, tend to be more easily detected by existing models. To investigate this, we examine how the text prompts for generation and image characteristics influence both quality scores and detector accuracy. We observe that images from short prompts tend to achieve higher preference scores while being easier to detect. Furthermore, through clustering and regression analyses, we verify that image characteristics like saturation, contrast, and texture richness collectively impact both image quality and detector accuracy. Finally, we demonstrate that the performance of off-the-shelf detectors can be enhanced across diverse generators and datasets by selecting input patches based on the predicted scores of our regression models, thus substantiating the broader applicability of our findings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Coxy7/AIGI-Detection-Quality-Paradox.

canonical_identity.abstract: Detecting fake images is becoming a major goal of computer vision. This need is becoming more and more pressing with the continuous improvement of synthesis methods based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), and even more with the appearance of powerful methods based on Diffusion Models (DM). Towards this end, it is important to gain insight into which image features better discriminate fake images from real ones. In this paper we report on our systematic study of a large number of image generators of different families, aimed at discovering the most forensically relevant characteristics of real and generated images. Our experiments provide a number of interesting observations and shed light on some intriguing properties of synthetic images: (1) not only the GAN models but also the DM and VQ-GAN (Vector Quantized Generative Adversarial Networks) models give rise to visible artifacts in the Fourier domain and exhibit anomalous regular patterns in the autocorrelation; (2) when the dataset used to train the model lacks sufficient variety, its biases can be transferred to the generated images; (3) synthetic and real images exhibit significant differences in the mid-high frequency signal content, observable in their radial and angular spectral power distributions.

data/curated/papers.csv.abstract: Detecting fake images is becoming a major goal of computer vision. This need is becoming more and more pressing with the continuous improvement of synthesis methods based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), and even more with the appearance of powerful methods based on Diffusion Models (DM). Towards this end, it is important to gain insight into which image features better discriminate fake images from real ones. In this paper we report on our systematic study of a large number of image generators of different families, aimed at discovering the most forensically relevant characteristics of real and generated images. Our experiments provide a number of interesting observations and shed light on some intriguing properties of synthetic images: (1) not only the GAN models but also the DM and VQ-GAN (Vector Quantized Generative Adversarial Networks) models give rise to visible artifacts in the Fourier domain and exhibit anomalous regular patterns in the autocorrelation; (2) when the dataset used to train the model lacks sufficient variety, its biases can be transferred to the generated images; (3) synthetic and real images exhibit significant differences in the mid-high frequency signal content, observable in their radial and angular spectral power distributions.

scientific_findings: The contribution statements on PDF pages 2-3 and the conclusion on page 8 identify systematic original observations about architectural traces, transferred training-data biases and deviations from natural-image spectra.

Section 4 specifies source-level second-order statistics, existing Zhang denoising with sigma=1, and 1000 images per source. Equations 1-9 and Figures 1-7 evaluate measurements rather than an independently proposed deployable classifier.

The conclusion explicitly places forensic detector design in future work. The complete main paper supplies no independently evaluated new detection decision rule, learned classifier, ROC/AUC/F1 or accuracy table.

The systematic analytical protocol is reproducible in outline, but reproducibility and the application of standard signal-processing measurements do not themselves establish substantive technical novelty under locked R4.

Table 1 contains 15 named model rows across GAN, VQ, diffusion and latent-diffusion groups. Variants and different training datasets prevent equating that row count to exactly 15 experimental sources.
Figure 3 compares latent upsampling factors 4 and 8, with spectral multiples 1/4 and 1/8. Training datasets also differ; this is not an isolated causal intervention on a single parameter.
Figure 4 explicitly labels rescaling factors 2.0, 1.4 and 0.7 and JPEG qualities 99, 95 and 75. It shows changes in source autocorrelation, not numerical detector robustness rates.

Figure 5 visibly contains ADM, Latent Diffusion and ImageNet/LSUN-bedroom source autocorrelations. The text describes JPEG quality 75 and its caption an 8x8 grid. Extraneous 'compressed UCID' strings in extracted PDF text are not a visibly plotted control and are not used as evidence.

Figure 6 compares radial distributions for ImageNet, FFHQ and LAION groups. Although the text claims matching training sources, Table 1 marks DALL-E 2 and eDiff-I training data unknown. Exact training-source equivalence is not independently established for every plotted model.

Radial statistics use 128 steps over 0-0.5 and focus on 0.2-0.5; angular statistics use 16 steps over 0-pi with a 0.1 high-pass cutoff. Figure 7 uses the signed standardized difference printed in Equation 9, described by the authors as the square root of Fisher's discriminant ratio.

Figures 6-7 contain quantitative curves without exact tabulated per-model point scores or classifier metrics. No numerical curve samples, p-values, confidence intervals, or causal effects are invented.

FFHQ interpolation/low-pass filtering, unknown training details and post-processing confounding bound the findings. The paper does not document a universally harmonized resolution/compression/prompt protocol across every model.

data/curated/papers.csv.abstract: Detecting fake images is becoming a major goal of computer vision. This need is becoming more and more pressing with the continuous improvement of synthesis methods based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), and even more with the appearance of powerful methods based on Diffusion Models (DM). Towards this end, it is important to gain insight into which image features better discriminate fake images from real ones. In this paper we report on our systematic study of a large number of image generators of different families, aimed at discovering the most forensically relevant characteristics of real and generated images. Our experiments provide a number of interesting observations and shed light on some intriguing properties of synthetic images: (1) not only the GAN models but also the DM and VQ-GAN (Vector Quantized Generative Adversarial Networks) models give rise to visible artifacts in the Fourier domain and exhibit anomalous regular patterns in the autocorrelation; (2) when the dataset used to train the model lacks sufficient variety, its biases can be transferred to the generated images; (3) synthetic and real images exhibit significant differences in the mid-high frequency signal content, observable in their radial and angular spectral power distributions.

analysis_study_assessment.confidence: High within the reviewed main paper.
analysis_study_assessment.positive_evidence: The principal contribution list comprises three original forensic observations; Sec4 systematically compares source-level second-order statistics over GAN/VQ/pixel-DM/latent-DM models and multiple real-source datasets. Eqs1-9,1000-image averages, manipulation conditions, matched-source comparisons and normalized variance-based angular curves provide more than isolated example-image anecdotes.
analysis_study_assessment.independence_from_method_validation: The experiments investigate synthesis artifacts, preprocessing confounds, training-data bias and fidelity to natural-image statistics as the paper's scientific objectives; they are not merely ablations supporting a newly proposed detector.

method_specific_assessment.confidence: High but bounded to the complete reviewed official main paper and locked R4 definition.
method_specific_assessment.new_deployable_detector: No deployable image-level decision procedure, thresholds or independently scored detector is introduced/evaluated in the main paper.
method_specific_assessment.new_learned_classifier: No new forensic classifier architecture, training objective or held-out classifier experiment is specified. Descriptions of GAN discriminators and generative models in Sec3 concern studied source models, not a newly contributed forensic classifier.
method_specific_assessment.new_forensic_representation: The paper applies descriptive source statistics to reveal new forensic observations. It does not separately claim and independently validate a substantively novel representation/algorithm as a technical contribution.
method_specific_assessment.reproducible_analysis_procedure: Yes: the measurement equations and settings operationalize much of the study. Reproducibility of an analysis alone does not establish technical novelty under R4. The assessment does not rest solely on the absence of a learned detector.

strong_positive_boundary.quote: In future work we will pursue the design of forensic detectors based also on these traces.
strong_positive_boundary.interpretation: The authors locate design of detectors exploiting these findings in future work. Combined with the stated observation-based contributions and standard measurement pipeline, this supports analysis-only research type.

method_specific_assessment.contrary_evidence_considered: Sec2 says this work uses second-order statistics to better expose synthesis patterns, and Sec4 specifies a reusable measurement procedure. These are acknowledged as technical analytical work. No independently claimed/evaluated substantive novelty in that procedure is established by the complete paper; the original scientific contribution is the observations obtained with it.
method_specific_assessment.independent_quantitative_method_evaluati: No method-versus-baseline detection accuracy/AUC/F1/operating-point/runtime table is reported. Table1 is a generator-property inventory. Figures1-7 contain image/statistical observations, transformation settings and spectral curves, not performance evaluation of a newly proposed forensic algorithm.

structured_quantitative_findings.locator: PDFp1/printed973 Fig1; PDFp2/974 Fig2; PDFp3/975 contribution list
structured_quantitative_findings.measurement: Source-average noise-residual power spectra and autocorrelations across generator families.
structured_quantitative_findings.finding_reported: Visible spectral peaks or regular autocorrelation patterns persist across the examined GAN, VQ and diffusion sources; weak spectral peaks alone do not establish artifact-free synthesis.
structured_quantitative_findings.quantitative_basis: Source-level second-order measurements use I=1000 images (Sec4). Figures1-2 show maps, not per-image detector scores.
structured_quantitative_findings.limitations: This is a reported observation on examined sources, not a proof that every future generator necessarily leaves a usable fingerprint.

structured_quantitative_findings.measurement: Residual power spectra and autocorrelation for three latent diffusion configurations.
structured_quantitative_findings.finding_reported: Factor4 configurations show spectral peaks at multiples of1/4 and periodicity4; factor8 shows denser spectral peaks at multiples of1/8 and sparser spatial repetitions.
structured_quantitative_findings.causal_limit: Factor and training data change together. This is not an isolated controlled causal ablation of upsampling factor. The paper attributes small differences between first two configurations mainly to training data.

structured_quantitative_findings.locator: PDFp5/977 Sec4.1 continuation; PDFp6/978 Fig4 and left-column text
structured_quantitative_findings.measurement: Stable Diffusion residual-autocorrelation changes under post-processing.
structured_quantitative_findings.finding_reported: Post-processing changes the observed maps, and stronger JPEG artifacts can conceal the original generation pattern.
structured_quantitative_findings.quantitative_boundary: The numbers are transformation settings. No accuracy, AUC, F1, robustness rate, error bar or runtime is reported for a detector in this figure. Blur/sharpening kernels and all implementation settings are not specified.

structured_quantitative_findings.measurement: ADM and Latent Diffusion residual autocorrelations compared with their real training-source examples.
structured_quantitative_findings.finding_reported: The LSUN-bedroom example has visible JPEG-like8x8 patterns in both real training data and generated data; these JPEG traces are much weaker in the ImageNet case and not transferred visibly in the same way. Prose reports that the biased training dataset was entirely compressed atQ75.
structured_quantitative_findings.source_inference_boundary: Training-pipeline provenance is the authors' reported explanation; the review did not download or independently audit the training images. Do not generalize this result to every generator/dataset.
structured_quantitative_findings.extraction_warning: pypdf text contains compressed UCID strings, but the rendered final Figure5 contains only the three visible columns above. UCID is not claimed as a plotted control or reviewed dataset.

structured_quantitative_findings.locator: PDFp6/978 Sec4.3; PDFp7/979 Eq7 and Fig6
structured_quantitative_findings.measurement: Radial spectral statistics averaged by source and compared with natural-image spectral decay.
structured_quantitative_findings.finding_reported: Real-source curves approximately follow the reference power-law shape; synthetic-source curves deviate across parts of the frequency range. The authors describe richer real-image intermediate-frequency content in many, but not all, cases.
structured_quantitative_findings.exception_reported: Some FFHQ synthetic curves fit the real-source curve closely; the paper attributes this to interpolation/low-pass filtering of FFHQ real images. StyleGAN2 and StyleGAN3 are noted as relatively good spectral matches.
structured_quantitative_findings.control_claim_and_limit: Sec4.3 describes matching real-source training data. That control is incompletely documented for the LAION/text-to-image group: Table1 lists different training corpora for several models and Unknown for DALL-E2/eDiff-I. No uniform matched training-data control is asserted by this review.
structured_quantitative_findings.numeric_boundary: The plotted curves have no tabulated per-frequency values or detector results. No exact plotted ordinate, effect size or detection improvement is inferred by digitization.

structured_quantitative_findings.measurement: Angular spectral statistics and signed standardized synthetic-versus-real mean differences at each direction.
structured_quantitative_findings.source_name: The paper calls Eq9 the square-root of Fisher's discriminant ratios.
structured_quantitative_findings.finding_reported: Polar curves expose anisotropy and real/synthetic angular-distribution differences, with the FFHQ interpolation caveat again applying. The related-work discussion identifies difficulty reproducing diagonal details.
structured_quantitative_findings.metric_boundary: Eq9 is signed and descriptive of labeled source populations. It is not an independently evaluated per-image classifier, calibrated authenticity score, ROC/AUC, significance test or operating-point analysis. No exact chart-point values are invented.

contradictions_and_limitations.finding: The authors describe using the same real source as generator training data, but Table1 reports Unknown training data for DALL-E2/eDiff-I and lists other corpora for some LAION-group models. Do not assert perfectly matched training data throughout.
Upsampling factor4 versus8 is demonstrated with different training sources, so the plotted association is not an isolated causal intervention.
Resize/JPEG examples expose map sensitivity, without reporting classifier robustness rates or proving downstream forensic reliability.
The reported LSUN-bedroom Q75 example illustrates a possible confound; it is not evidence that every generator copies a JPEG fingerprint.

Some FFHQ synthetic curves approximate real spectra; authors attribute this to interpolation/low-pass filtering of real data. The paper does not show a perfectly preprocessing-controlled universal separation.

contradictions_and_limitations.issue: No inference from descriptive plots to detector performance
contradictions_and_limitations.finding: No classifier split, ROC/AUC/F1, false-positive operating point, confidence interval or p-value is reported. Source-mean curves and Fisher-style quantities are not detector accuracies.
Printed notation and signed Eq9 naming are preserved; no undocumented numerical correction or digitized exact plot value is claimed.
Compressed UCID strings occur in text extraction but not the visible rendered final figure. The review uses the rendered columns/caption.

Only the official CVF workshop accepted-version source is reviewed. Canonical CVPR-main metadata discrepancy is noted without modifying it or resolving P566; no IEEE-final/arXiv equivalence is presumed.
